effect_vs_control: antiparallel beta sheet 24.2% (PF4 alone) -> 35.8% with 5 ug/mL aptamer; heparin at 6.9 ug/mL gave 34.3%
source_table: Fig 5A (values in Results, 'Aptamer-induced changes in PF4 resemble those induced by heparin')
notes: Text: 'Deconvolution of the spectra of PF4 obtained after the addition of 5 ug/mL 44mer-DNA protein C aptamer or 6.9 ug/mL heparin showed an increase in anti-parallel b sheet content from 24.2% to 34.3% for heparin and to 35.8% for the 44mer-DNA protein C aptamer. This refolding was balanced by a decrease of the a helix fraction from 12.2% to 8.9% (heparin) and to 8.1% (44mer) and a decrease in the b-turn fraction from 22.8% to 19.8% (heparin) and 20.5% (44mer). Parallel b sheet and random coil content did not change significantly.' Most pronounced alterations over a broader aptamer range (5-20 ug/mL) than heparin (6.9-7.2 ug/mL). Cell-free mechanistic row: this is the neoepitope-forming conformational change, but NO platelet endpoint was measured, so grade 0 per the convention applied to all cell-free rows here. DISCREPANCY: Methods states PF4 at 40 ug/mL for CD; the Fig 5A legend states PF4 at 20 ug/mL.

effect_vs_control: increasing ISIS 2302 concentrations progressively eluted Factor H
notes: IN-VITRO MECHANISM ROW — cell-free binding competition, NOT a platelet assay; grade 0 is a schema floor, not an observed platelet null. species=NA because the abstract does NOT state the species of the Factor H used; it was NOT assumed to be human, which matters because a human-source in-vitro row would otherwise be miscounted toward this lane's human-data priority. Verbatim basis: 'Direct interaction between ISIS 2302 and Factor H was demonstrated in a competition assay, where increasing concentrations of ISIS 2302 eluted Factor H from a heparin-sepharose column.' No concentrations, IC50 or elution percentages appear in the abstract, hence dose and readout_value TBD. Mechanistically this is polyanion competition for the heparin-binding site of Factor H — the same physicochemical PS-polyanion property invoked for platelet-protein binding, which is why the row is worth carrying despite not being platelet-specific.
